name: Cradle Mountain
tagline: Jagged dolerite peaks, glacial lakes and wombats in a Tasmanian Wilderness World Heritage park.
description: Cradle Mountain-Lake St Clair National Park sits in the Central Highlands, with the Cradle Mountain end in the north and Lake St Clair in the south, and no road joining the two. People come to walk among rainforest, buttongrass moorland and ancient pines, from short boardwalks to the multi-day Overland Track. Gustav Weindorfer built a chalet here in 1912 and campaigned for the area to become a national park for the people for all time. Wombats, wallabies and pademelons live in the park, and snow, rain and wind are possible at any time of year.

goodToKnow.title: Parks pass and shuttle
goodToKnow.detail: A valid Tasmanian parks pass is required to enter the national park. Private cars cannot enter during shuttle hours, so park at the Cradle Mountain Visitor Centre, validate your pass and take the shuttle to Dove Lake.

goodToKnow.title: Book the Overland Track
goodToKnow.detail: In the peak season, which runs from October to May, walkers must book, pay a track fee and walk north to south. Book well ahead.

goodToKnow.title: Pack for all weather
goodToKnow.detail: Weather can change very quickly, even in summer, so carry waterproofs and warm layers on every walk. Do not feed the wildlife, and keep food packed away because currawongs will open bags.

name: Devonport
tagline: The Spirit of Tasmania ferry port, with a lighthouse headland, penguins and the coast and hills of the north-west.
description: Devonport is the third-largest city in Tasmania, on the north-west coast, and the arrival port of the Spirit of Tasmania ferry from the mainland. It is the closest arrival point to Cradle Mountain, about an hour's drive away, and has its own lighthouse headland at Mersey Bluff, a maritime museum and an arboretum. Within a drive are the mural town of Sheffield, a steam railway, limestone caves and a canyon walk. Little penguins walk up the sand at Lillico Beach each evening.
whyVisit: See little penguins at Lillico Beach
whyVisitSubjects: little penguins on Lillico Beach

goodToKnow.title: Ferry terminal
goodToKnow.detail: The Spirit of Tasmania runs between Geelong and Devonport, and the terminal is in East Devonport, across the Mersey from the town centre. The walk round via the road bridge is long, so a car or taxi helps.

goodToKnow.title: Penguin etiquette
goodToKnow.detail: Little penguins walk up Lillico Beach each evening, and Mersey Bluff has a penguin-viewing area. Keep your distance and let them come ashore undisturbed.

goodToKnow.title: Hire a car for the area
goodToKnow.detail: The caves, Sheffield and Leven Canyon are out of town, and driving a private car is the easiest way to see them. Car rental is available at the wharf and the airport.

name: Wynyard
tagline: A small north-west coast town beneath Table Cape, with tulip fields and quiet beaches.
description: Wynyard is a small town on the Inglis River where the coast road meets Bass Strait. The volcanic headland of Table Cape rises behind it, with a lighthouse and fields that are planted with tulips for the spring bloom. To the west the road runs past Fossil Bluff and the coves of Boat Harbour and Sisters Beach into Rocky Cape National Park. It suits a slow day of coast and lookouts between Burnie and Stanley.
whyVisit: See Table Cape's spring tulip fields
whyVisitSubjects: tulip fields at Table Cape with lighthouse

goodToKnow.title: Tulip season is short
goodToKnow.detail: The tulips at Table Cape flower for about a month each spring, from late September to late October in 2026, and entry to the farm is charged. Check the farm's dates before you drive out.

goodToKnow.title: Parks pass for Rocky Cape
goodToKnow.detail: Rocky Cape National Park needs a valid Tasmanian parks pass for entry.

goodToKnow.title: Drive the coast
goodToKnow.detail: Buses run to Burnie and Launceston, but driving is the fastest and easiest way along this coast; fuel and food are easiest in Wynyard and Burnie.

name: Burnie
tagline: A working port city on Bass Strait with penguins at the foreshore and gardens and falls inland.
description: Burnie is a regional port city on Tasmania's north-west coast, with an industrial deep-water port and north-facing beaches. Little penguins come ashore at Parsonage Point, and the Emu Valley Rhododendron Garden and Guide Falls are a short drive south. The nearby town of Penguin has a giant penguin statue in its centre.

goodToKnow.title: Penguin viewing
goodToKnow.detail: Guides are at the Little Penguin Observation Centre around sunset from October to March, and viewing is free; confirm times before going.

goodToKnow.title: Falls are best after rain
goodToKnow.detail: Guide Falls flows best in winter and spring and can be modest after a dry summer.

goodToKnow.title: A car helps
goodToKnow.detail: The Emu Valley Rhododendron Garden is 6 km south of Burnie and Guide Falls about 20 minutes' drive south, so driving is the easiest way to reach them.

bestTimeBlurb: {months} cover the penguin season. The garden's rhododendrons peak from September to November, and Guide Falls runs strongest in winter and spring.

name: Mole Creek Karst National Park
tagline: Limestone country of show caves, glow-worms and a cliff-edge lookout below the Great Western Tiers.
description: Mole Creek Karst National Park was created to protect an underground landscape of caves, sinkholes, gorges and streams that run below the surface. Two show caves are open to visitors: Marakoopa, with its glow-worm display and the Great Cathedral cavern, and King Solomons, a compact, drier cave with shawls and stalactites. A scenic drive through Chudleigh, Mole Creek and Caveside adds to the visit, and Devils Gullet, near Mole Creek, is a lookout platform over a sheer cliff with views to Cradle Mountain. Deloraine is the gateway town, and many lesser caves are reserved for recreational cavers.

goodToKnow.title: Cave tours are guided
goodToKnow.detail: Entry to the caves is by guided tour only; the Underground Rivers and Glow Worms tour and the King Solomons tour suit all ages, but the Great Cathedral tour needs medium fitness.

goodToKnow.title: Pass and tickets
goodToKnow.detail: A parks pass is not needed to tour the show caves, but a pass lets you visit other scenic spots such as Croesus Reserve.

goodToKnow.title: Visitor centre hours
goodToKnow.detail: The visitor centre is open seven days, 9.30am to 4pm from October to April and 9.30am to 3.45pm from May to September, and closes at 2.30pm every third Tuesday of the month.

bestTimeBlurb: {months} suit the scenic drive and the walk to Croesus Reserve. The visitor centre is open seven days a week all year, so winter visits work too.

name: King Island
tagline: A windswept Bass Strait island of lighthouses, shipwreck history, surf beaches, cheese and crayfish.
description: King Island lies in Bass Strait between Tasmania and Victoria, and visitors reach it by air from Melbourne or Tasmania; there is no ferry. More than 60 ships are known to have been wrecked on its coast, and Cape Wickham Lighthouse, at 48 m Australia's tallest, stands at its northern tip; divers come for the wrecks. The pasture produces rich milk for the island's cheeses, and the island is also known for lobster. It has no traffic lights and few roads.

goodToKnow.title: Fly in
goodToKnow.detail: There is no ferry service, so book a flight to Currie from Melbourne, Hobart, Launceston or Burnie.

goodToKnow.title: Hire a car
goodToKnow.detail: There is no public transport on the island, and car hire is available in Currie; book it with your flights.

goodToKnow.title: Wind and cliffs
goodToKnow.detail: The island is windswept; stay back from cliff edges at Seal Rocks, where the cliffs rise about 60 m from the sea, and follow signs at lookouts and wreck sites.

bestTimeBlurb: {months} are the summer months, the usual choice for walking to the Calcified Forest and Seal Rocks; wind is common at any time of year.

name: Flinders Island
tagline: Granite peaks, white beaches and quiet history in the Furneaux Group.
description: Flinders Island is the largest of the 78 islands in the Furneaux Group in Bass Strait, and one of two Bass Strait islands open to everyday tourism, with scheduled flights from Launceston and Melbourne. Granite peaks in Strzelecki National Park rise above white beaches and calm snorkelling water. The island also holds Wybalenna, where Aboriginal Tasmanians were exiled in the 1830s and 1840s, and a museum covering the sealers and shipwrecks of Bass Strait. Whitemark is its largest town.
whyVisitSubjects: Strzelecki Peaks granite summit on Flinders Island

goodToKnow.title: Fly or sail
goodToKnow.detail: Flights run to Flinders Island Airport from Launceston and Melbourne, and a weekly freight barge from Bridport can carry cars; check schedules with the operators.

goodToKnow.title: Rent a car
goodToKnow.detail: There is no public transport; the B85 runs most of the island's length, and a hire car is the practical way to reach the peaks, beaches and Killiecrankie.

goodToKnow.title: Strzelecki is steep
goodToKnow.detail: The Strzelecki Peaks walk is a 4-5 hour return on a steep track; start early and carry water and a jacket.

bestTimeBlurb: {months} are the summer months, the usual choice for swimming and snorkelling at the beaches and for the Strzelecki Peaks climb.
